meta.title: Who really said "Contentment is natural wealth, luxury is artificial poverty"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Socrates. Joseph Addison coined 'luxury is artificial poverty' himself in The Spectator No. 574 (1714), adding it to a line he credited to Socrates.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Contentment is natural wealth, luxury is artificial poverty'?
meta.ogDescription: Addison's 1714 Spectator essay: 'Content is natural Wealth,' says Socrates; 'to which I shall add, Luxury is artificial Poverty.' Half the quote is his own.

answer.label: Not Socrates — actually Joseph Addison
answer.authorDates: 1672–1719 · English essayist & co-founder of The Spectator
answer.sourceLine: The couplet comes from Joseph Addison’s Spectator No. 574, published Friday, 30 July 1714. Addison credited only the first half to Socrates — “Content is natural Wealth, says Socrates; to which I shall add, Luxury is artificial Poverty ↗” — so the second half is Addison’s own invention, flagged as such in his own sentence. No surviving Greek source has been identified for the Socrates half either.

source.heading: The Spectator, No. 574

docMeta.dd: Friday, 30 July 1714 — part of the 1714 revival (Nos. 556–635), collected as volume eight
“Content is natural Wealth … Luxury is artificial Poverty” — not “Contentment”

source.excerpt: Let a Man’s Estate be what it will, he is a poor Man if he does not live within it, and naturally sets himself to Sale to any one that can give him his Price. … In short, Content is equivalent to Wealth, and Luxury to Poverty; or, to give the Thought a more agreeable Turn, Content is natural Wealth, says Socrates; to which I shall add, Luxury is artificial Poverty.
source.trailTitle: How a 1714 couplet became a Socrates quote
trail: 30 July 1714 — Joseph Addison publishes Spectator No. 574, an essay on contentment, ending with the couplet: “Content is natural Wealth, says Socrates; to which I shall add, Luxury is artificial Poverty.” Both halves are on the page, and so is the seam between them — Project Gutenberg ↗.

1852 — Charles Simmons’s A Laconic Manual and Brief Remarker (North Wrentham, Mass.), p. 103, reports the line as a single saying of Socrates, per Wikiquote ↗. Addison’s “I shall add” has vanished; the couplet now travels under one name.

Today — The fused version saturates quote sites and even exam essay prompts. Wikiquote ↗ keeps it in the “Attributed” column and states the original source is unknown. Quote Investigator has not published on this line.

The real Socratic version — For the thought with an actual citation behind it, go to Xenophon: Socrates tells Antiphon that “to have no wants is divine; to have as few as possible comes next to the divine” ↗ (Memorabilia 1.6.10).
source.excerptNote: Addison’s own sentence draws the line for us: the Socrates half is quoted, the luxury half is announced as an addition of his own. Spelling, capitalisation and italics follow the Project Gutenberg text of the collected Spectator — Addison set both halves in italics rather than quotation marks.

author.name: Joseph Addison
author.kicker: The man who actually wrote half of it
author.heading: Joseph Addison
author.metaLine: 1672–1719 · English essayist, poet & co-founder of The Spectator
author.bio: Joseph Addison was an English essayist, poet, playwright and politician who, with his friend Richard Steele, founded The Spectator in 1711. Its short daily essays — polished, conversational, morally observant — did more than almost any other writing of the age to shape English prose style. In No. 574 he did what the Spectator essays do best: he borrowed a saying he credited to Socrates and, quite openly, capped it with a line of his own manufacture.

misattribution.heading: How Addison’s couplet lost its second author
misattribution.intro: This is an unusually clean case, because the man who wrote the famous half told us he was writing it. Addison’s sentence contains its own attribution notice — and the internet has spent three centuries deleting it.

items.why: Quote sites present the line as a single Socratic saying. It is not: it is a two-part construction from an English essay of 1714, in which only the first part is credited to Socrates. Wikiquote ↗ places it under “Attributed” — its section for quotes whose sources cannot be verified.

Addison wrote, verbatim: “Content is natural Wealth, says Socrates; to which I shall add, Luxury is artificial Poverty.” The words “to which I shall add” are an explicit claim of authorship. No Greek source has been identified for this half — Addison announces it as his own addition: read it in No. 574 ↗.

Addison credited this half to Socrates, but named no work, and no passage in Plato, Xenophon or any surviving source has been matched to it. Wikiquote ↗ states plainly that the original source of the statement is unknown.

Addison wrote “Content is natural Wealth.” The version that circulates today reads “Contentment…” and welds the two halves into one sentence under one name. The earliest instance Wikiquote ↗ cites of the fused, Socrates-only form is Charles Simmons’s A Laconic Manual and Brief Remarker (1852), p. 103 — though Wikiquote notes the original source of the statement is unknown.

misattribution.truthLine: The line the internet hands to Socrates is really Joseph Addison’s 1714 couplet — one half borrowed from an unlocatable saying, one half written by Addison and signposted as his. The Spectator, No. 574 ↗.

context.heading: An essay against “the chace after imaginary Pleasures”
lead: Addison’s No. 574 is an essay on contentment, written for the revived Spectator of 1714. Its argument is that wealth is a ratio, not a sum: “there are none can be properly called rich, who have not more than they want.” The rich, he says, live in “a kind of splendid Poverty,” perpetually wanting because they measure themselves against those ahead of them rather than against what they already hold.

The famous couplet is the essay’s rhetorical flourish — and Addison shows his workings. He first states the plain version (“Content is equivalent to Wealth, and Luxury to Poverty”), then offers to “give the Thought a more agreeable Turn” by pairing a Socratic tag with a matching phrase of his own. The elegance that made the line quotable is precisely the part Addison built himself.
context.detailsSummary: So did Socrates think anything like this?
detailsBody: Yes — the idea is genuinely Socratic, even if this wording is not. In Xenophon’s Memorabilia, Socrates answers the sophist Antiphon, who has mocked his poverty, with a real and well-sourced line: “to have no wants is divine; to have as few as possible comes next to the divine” ↗ (Memorabilia 1.6.10, trans. E. C. Marchant).

That is the durable Socratic thought Addison was reaching for. But it is a different sentence, from a different author, in a different language — and it is the one that actually has a citation behind it.
context.pull: “Content is natural Wealth,” says Socrates; to which I shall add, “Luxury is artificial Poverty.”
